verse.text: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the chosen who live as temporary residents of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,
verse.note: The word describes someone staying for a time in a place that is not their home, without implying banishment, which “exiles” now suggests. The Septuagint uses it of Abraham among the Hittites. Scholars debate whether Peter describes his readers’ actual social standing, their spiritual condition as people whose home is elsewhere, or both.

This was the established term for Jews living scattered outside the land of Israel. Peter applies it to communities in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor (modern Turkey) that, judging from the rest of the letter, included many non-Jews. The readers are being addressed in Israel’s own vocabulary.

verse.text: chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through being made holy by the Spirit, for obedience and sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you.

note.term: for obedience and sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ

verse.note: The image recalls Exodus 24, where the people pledge obedience and Moses sprinkles them with the blood of the covenant. The Greek leaves open whether “of Jesus Christ” belongs only to the blood or also to the obedience (“obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling with his blood”).

verse.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who in his great mercy has caused us to be born anew into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in the heavens for you,
verse.note: The Greek is plural here, a Semitic turn of phrase for God’s dwelling that most translations flatten to “heaven.” The plural is kept where the Greek has it; in verse 12 the Greek is singular.

verse.text: who are being guarded by God’s power through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.
In this you rejoice, though now for a little while, if it must be, you have been grieved by various trials,
verse.note: “In this” most likely refers to the whole prospect described in verses 3–5, but the Greek could also mean “in him” (God or Christ) or “at that time,” that is, the last time. The verb can also be read as a command, “rejoice,” though most take it as a statement.
Older versions have “temptations,” but the word here means hardships that put faith to the proof, not enticements to sin. Most modern translations already use “trials” in this verse.

verse.text: so that the tested genuineness of your faith—more precious than gold, which perishes even though it is tested by fire—may be found to bring praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.
Though you have not seen him, you love him; though you do not see him now, you believe in him and rejoice with a joy that is beyond words and filled with glory,
as you receive the outcome of your faith, the salvation of your souls.
It was about this salvation that the prophets who prophesied of the grace meant for you sought and searched intently,

searching to find what time or what kind of time the Spirit of Christ within them was pointing to in testifying beforehand to the sufferings destined for Christ and the glories that would follow them.

note.term: what time or what kind of time

verse.note: The first Greek pronoun can be read with “time,” as here, or on its own as “whom,” giving “what person or time,” which several major translations adopt. Both are grammatically sound and scholars are divided. The reading chosen keeps the focus on timing, which the following words about sufferings and later glories develop.

verse.text: It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you in these things, which have now been announced to you through those who brought you the good news by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven—things into which angels long to look.
verse.note: “Gospel” has become a religious term and a book title. The Greek verb was an ordinary one for announcing good news publicly, and many modern translations already alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

verse.text: Therefore, having dressed your minds for action and keeping sober, set your hope fully on the grace being brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.

note.term: having dressed your minds for action
note.traditional: gird up the loins of your mind

verse.note: The Greek is literally “having girded up the loins of your mind.” The picture is of tucking a long robe into the belt so as to move freely for work or travel. It may echo the Passover instruction in Exodus 12:11 to eat with loins girded, ready to depart. Most modern translations also replace the idiom with an equivalent such as “prepare your minds for action.”

The adverb “fully” stands between two verbs in Greek and could go with either. Most translations attach it to hoping, as here; a number of scholars attach it to the preceding word, giving “keeping perfectly sober, set your hope.”

verse.text: As children of obedience, do not conform to the desires you once had in your ignorance,
but, as the one who called you is holy, be holy yourselves in your whole way of life,
for it is written, “You shall be holy, because I am holy.”
And if you call on as Father the one who judges impartially according to each person’s work, live in fear throughout the time of your stay as foreigners,
knowing that it was not with perishable things, silver or gold, that you were ransomed from the empty way of life handed down by your ancestors,
but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.
He was foreknown before the foundation of the world but was made manifest at the end of the times for the sake of you
who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God.
Having purified your souls by obedience to the truth so as to have sincere brotherly love, love one another earnestly from the heart,
verse.note: Many manuscripts read “from a pure heart,” and many translations follow them; the Greek text translated here has the shorter reading. The evidence is closely balanced, and other critical editions print “pure” in brackets. Some later manuscripts also add “through the Spirit” after “obedience to the truth.”

verse.text: for you have been born anew, not from perishable seed but from imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God.

note.term: the living and enduring word of God

verse.note: The Greek word order allows “living and enduring” to describe either the word or God (“the word of the living and enduring God”). Most translators take it of the word, because the quotation that follows says that the word of the Lord endures.

verse.text: For “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers and the flower falls,

note.term: “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers and the flower falls,

verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 40:6–8 in a form close to the Greek Septuagint. “All flesh” is a Hebrew way of saying all humankind in its frailty. The passage opens Isaiah’s announcement of good news to exiles, and Peter picks up that theme in the next verse.

verse.text: but the word of the Lord endures forever.” And this is the word that was announced to you as good news.
So put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander,
and, like newborn babies, long for the pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow up into salvation,

note.traditional: sincere milk of the word (KJV); pure spiritual milk

verse.note: The Greek adjective (logikos) meant “rational” or “belonging to the realm of mind and spirit” in this period, marking the milk as non-literal; most modern versions have “spiritual.” Because Peter has just spoken of God’s living word (1:23–25), others translate “milk of the word.” It is a different Greek word from the “spiritual” of verse 5.

verse.text: if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good.
As you come to him, a living stone, rejected by people but chosen and honored in God’s sight,
verse.note: The Greek word means both “valuable” and “held in honor.” “Honored” is used here and in verse 6 because verse 7 picks the word up with its related noun (“the honor is for you who believe”) and sets it against being “put to shame.” Most translations have “precious,” which suits a stone but hides that link.

verse.text: you too, like living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verse.note: The Greek form can be a statement (“you are being built up”) or a command (“let yourselves be built up”). Most translators and commentators take it as a statement, as here; a minority prefer the command.

verse.text: For it stands in Scripture: “Look, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and honored, and whoever believes in him will never be put to shame.”
So the honor is for you who believe; but for those who do not believe, “The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner,”
and “a stone that makes people stumble and a rock that makes people fall.” They stumble because they disobey the word, and to this they were also appointed.

note.term: a rock that makes people fall

verse.note: The word means a trap or obstacle that brings someone down, not an injury to the feelings, which is what “offense” now suggests. The phrase quotes Isaiah 8:14. Several modern versions render it much as here, while others keep “rock of offense.”

verse.text: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, so that you may proclaim the mighty acts of the one who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.
verse.note: Greek has one word (ethnos) for “nation” and, in the plural, for the non-Jewish peoples. It is translated “nation” here, where a title of Israel from Exodus 19:6 is applied to the readers, and “Gentiles” in verse 12, where it refers to the unbelieving society around them.

verse.text: Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.
Beloved, I urge you, as foreigners and temporary residents, to keep away from the desires of the flesh, which wage war against the soul.

note.traditional: strangers and pilgrims (KJV); aliens and exiles; sojourners and exiles

verse.note: The first word names a foreigner living in a place without citizen rights; the second, a person staying somewhere for a time. Neither implies banishment, as “exiles” does, or a religious journey, as “pilgrims” does. The pair echoes Abraham’s description of himself in Genesis 23:4; whether Peter means the readers’ actual social standing, a figure for their life in the world, or both, is debated.

verse.text: Let your conduct among the Gentiles be good, so that, where they slander you as evildoers, they may observe your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation.
verse.note: In Scripture a “visitation” is God’s coming to inspect, which brings rescue or judgment depending on what he finds. Most interpreters take this as the final day of judgment; some think of the moment when God brings an unbeliever to faith.

verse.text: Submit to every human institution for the Lord’s sake, whether to the king as supreme,

note.traditional: every ordinance of man (KJV); every human institution

verse.note: Elsewhere in the New Testament this noun means “creation” or “creature,” and a number of scholars translate “every human creature,” that is, every person, with king and governors as examples. Most translations take it as an authority established among humans, drawing on the word’s use for the founding of cities, and that reading is followed here.

In the Greek-speaking eastern provinces the Roman emperor was commonly called “king,” and the emperor is meant here; several modern versions translate “emperor.” The governors of the next verse are the officials who administered the provinces under him.

verse.text: or to governors as sent by him to punish evildoers and to praise those who do good
(for this is God’s will: that by doing good you silence the ignorance of foolish people).
Live as free people, yet do not use your freedom as a cover for evil; live as God’s slaves.
Honor everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the king.
Household slaves, submit to your masters with all fear, not only to those who are good and considerate but also to those who are crooked.
verse.note: The word denotes slaves attached to a household, not hired staff; the beatings mentioned in verse 20 reflect their legal position. Older versions have “servants,” which now suggests paid employment.

note.traditional: with all fear; with all respect

verse.note: Since the previous verse reserves fear for God and gives the king only honor, many interpreters take this as fear of God, not dread of the master. Others, with the translations that have “with all respect,” take it as deference toward the master.

verse.text: For this finds favor: if someone, mindful of God, bears up under pain while suffering unjustly.
verse.note: The Greek says simply “this is charis,” the word usually translated “grace,” and verse 20 repeats it with “with God.” Most take it here as what wins God’s favor or approval. A minority read “this is grace,” meaning that such endurance is God’s grace at work.

verse.text: For what credit is there if you sin and are beaten and endure it? But if you do good and suffer and endure it, this finds favor with God.
For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his footsteps.
He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.
When he was insulted, he did not insult in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judges justly.
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two. “Justly” here and “righteousness” in verse 24 share a single root, as do “just” and “righteous” elsewhere.

verse.text: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that, dead to sins, we might live for righteousness. By his wounds you were healed.
verse.note: The word means wood or something made of wood, and was used for a stake or gallows as well as for a tree; here it is the cross. “Tree” is kept because the wording echoes Deuteronomy 21:22–23, where a body hung on a “tree” is under God’s curse (compare Galatians 3:13).

verse.text: For you were like sheep going astray, but now you have turned back to the shepherd and overseer of your souls.
In the same way, wives, submit to your own husbands, so that even if some of them disobey the word, they may be won over without a word by the conduct of their wives,
when they observe your pure and reverent conduct.
Let your adornment not be the outward kind—braiding hair, putting on gold jewelry, or wearing clothes—
but the hidden person of the heart, with the imperishable quality of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is of great value in God’s sight.
verse.note: “Meek” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes someone who is gentle and not self-assertive, and “gentle” or “humble” is the mainstream modern rendering. The related noun is rendered “gentleness” in verse 16.

verse.text: For this is how the holy women of the past who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, submitting to their own husbands,
as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. You have become her children if you do good and do not fear anything that terrifies.

note.traditional: as long as ye do well

verse.note: The Greek has two participles (“doing good and not fearing”) whose relation to “you have become her children” is left open. They may state a condition, as here and in most translations, or describe how the readers show themselves her children (“by doing good”). Sarah calls Abraham “lord” in Genesis 18:12, and the closing words echo Proverbs 3:25.

verse.text: Husbands, in the same way, live with your wives with understanding, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, and as fellow heirs also of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.
verse.note: “Vessel” was a familiar image for a human being as a created, fragile thing, or for the body. The comparative “weaker” implies that the husband is a vessel too. The weakness is usually understood as physical strength or social vulnerability rather than moral or intellectual inferiority, and the verse goes on to call wives “fellow heirs.” Some translations paraphrase as “the weaker partner.”

verse.text: Finally, all of you, be of one mind, sympathetic, loving toward your brothers and sisters, tenderhearted, and humble,
not repaying evil with evil or insult with insult, but on the contrary blessing, because you were called to this, so that you might inherit a blessing.
For “Whoever wants to love life and see good days must keep the tongue from evil and the lips from speaking deceit,
verse.note: Verses 10–12 quote Psalm 34:12–16 (33:13–17 in the Septuagint numbering) with small adaptations and without an introductory formula. The opening “For” is the letter’s own link to the preceding instruction.

text.q: must turn away from evil and do good, must seek peace and pursue it.
For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their plea, but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

verse.text: And who is going to harm you if you become zealous for what is good?
But even if you should suffer because of righteousness, you are blessed. Have no fear of them, and do not be troubled,

note.traditional: be not afraid of their terror

verse.note: Literally “do not fear their fear.” The words come from Isaiah 8:12, where the sense is “do not fear what this people fears,” and some translations keep that sense here. In this context of hostility most interpreters take it as “do not be afraid of them” or “of their threats.” Isaiah continues “the Lord himself you shall regard as holy,” which the next verse applies to Christ.

verse.text: but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always ready to make a defense to anyone who asks you for an account of the hope that is in you,

note.term: honor Christ the Lord as holy
note.traditional: sanctify the Lord God; sanctify Christ as Lord

verse.note: The traditional “sanctify” hides the link with “holy,” and Christ cannot be made holy; the sense, as the standard lexicons give it, is to acknowledge and treat as holy. The Greek can also be construed “honor Christ as Lord,” as several translations have it. The wording adapts Isaiah 8:13, where “the Lord” is Israel’s God.

Later manuscripts read “the Lord God” instead of “the Lord Christ,” and that reading lies behind the King James Version. The earliest witnesses have “Christ,” and modern critical editions follow them.

verse.text: but with gentleness and reverence, keeping a good conscience, so that those who disparage your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame in the very matter in which you are slandered.
For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God’s will, than for doing evil.
For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring you to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,
verse.note: Many manuscripts, including early ones, read “died” in place of “suffered,” and the manuscripts are also divided between “bring you to God” and “bring us to God.” The edition translated here reads “suffered” and “you.” “Suffered” fits the letter’s usual vocabulary and the argument of verse 17, and the verse in any case goes on to speak of Christ being put to death.

The Greek sets “flesh” and “spirit” in exact parallel, with no preposition. The phrase may mean that Christ was made alive in the realm of the spirit, that is, in his risen mode of existence, or that he was made alive by God’s Spirit (“by the Spirit”). The parallel with “in the flesh” favors the first. Many recent interpreters take “made alive” to refer to the resurrection.

verse.text: in which he also went and made proclamation to the spirits in prison,

note.traditional: preached unto the spirits in prison

verse.note: This is one of the most disputed verses in the New Testament. The most widely held scholarly view today is that the “spirits” are the rebellious angelic beings of Genesis 6:1–4, whose imprisonment is described in Jewish writings such as 1 Enoch, and that the risen Christ announced his victory to them. Others take them to be the human dead of Noah’s generation, or hold that Christ preached through Noah to people now in prison. The verb means “proclaim” and does not say what was announced; “in which” could also be read “at which time.”

verse.text: who had once disobeyed, when God’s patience waited in the days of Noah while an ark was being built, in which a few—that is, eight people—were saved through water.
verse.note: The Greek word often rendered “soul” is used here, as frequently in the Septuagint, simply to count individuals. “Souls” could suggest to a modern reader that only an immaterial part of them was rescued. Most modern translations have “persons” or “people.”

verse.text: Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you as well—not the removal of dirt from the flesh but the pledge of a good conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,

note.term: the pledge of a good conscience toward God
note.traditional: the answer of a good conscience toward God; an appeal to God for a good conscience

verse.note: The noun occurs only here in the New Testament and its meaning is disputed. It is related to a verb meaning “ask,” which supports “appeal” or “request”: baptism as an appeal to God for a good conscience. In papyri, mostly somewhat later, the word-group is used of the formal question and answer that sealed a contract, which supports “pledge”: a commitment made to God from, or to keep, a good conscience. Both renderings have strong scholarly support, and the choice here is not certain.

verse.text: who is at God’s right hand, having gone into heaven, with angels and authorities and powers made subject to him.
Since, then, Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same way of thinking, because the one who has suffered in the flesh is finished with sin,

note.term: because the one who has suffered in the flesh is finished with sin
note.traditional: for he that hath suffered in the flesh hath ceased from sin

verse.note: The Greek connective can mean “because”, giving the reason for arming oneself, or “that”, giving the content of the “way of thinking”. It is also disputed who “the one who has suffered” is: the believer who has accepted suffering and so broken with sin, the believer united with Christ’s death in baptism, or Christ himself. The rendering leaves that open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: so as to live the remaining time in the flesh no longer by human cravings but by the will of God.
For the time that has passed was enough for carrying out what the Gentiles want, living in debauchery, cravings, drunkenness, revels, drinking parties, and forbidden idolatries.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary plural “nations”, which in Jewish usage meant the non-Jewish peoples. The readers seem to have been largely non-Jews themselves, yet the letter uses the word for outsiders whose way of life they have left behind.

verse.text: In this they find it strange that you do not run with them into the same flood of dissipation, and so they slander you.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the source of English “blaspheme”, but in the period it meant abusive or defamatory speech against anyone. The verb has no object here; most translations supply “you” and understand abuse of the believers, as this one does. Some interpreters take it as blasphemy against God.

verse.text: But they will give an account to the one who stands ready to judge the living and the dead.
For this is why the good news was announced to the dead as well: so that, though judged in the flesh by human standards, they might live in the spirit by God’s standard.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for announcing good news. “Gospel” has become a religious term or a book title in English, so “good news” is used for this word family throughout. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

Most scholars today take “the dead” to be believers who heard the good news while alive and have since died: human judgment condemned them, but they live before God. Others connect the verse with the proclamation to the spirits in 3:19 and understand a proclamation made to people already dead. The phrases rendered “by human standards” and “by God’s standard” are literally “according to humans” and “according to God”, and “in the spirit” could also be read as “by the Spirit”.

verse.text: The end of all things has come near. So be sensible and sober for the sake of your prayers.
Above all, keep your love for one another constant, because love covers a multitude of sins.

note.term: love covers a multitude of sins
note.traditional: charity shall cover the multitude of sins

verse.note: This echoes Proverbs 10:12 in a form close to the Hebrew, not the Greek Septuagint; the same saying appears in James 5:20. In Proverbs the point is that love overlooks and forgives the wrongs of others instead of stirring up conflict, which fits the context of community life here.

verse.text: Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
As each one has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God’s varied grace.

If anyone speaks, let it be as speaking oracles of God; if anyone serves, as serving from the strength that God supplies, so that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.
Beloved, do not find it strange that a fire is burning among you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you.

note.term: a fire is burning among you

verse.note: The Greek noun means a burning and is used in the Septuagint for the smelting furnace that tests silver and gold (Proverbs 27:21), an image the letter already used at 1:7. The verse also plays on “strange”: the same verb describes the outsiders’ reaction in verse 4.

verse.text: Instead, insofar as you share in the sufferings of Christ, rejoice, so that at the revelation of his glory you may also rejoice and exult.
If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.

note.term: the Spirit of glory and of God
note.traditional: the spirit of glory and of God

verse.note: Some manuscripts add “and of power” after “glory”, and many later ones add at the end “on their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified”, which the King James Version includes. The shorter text is translated here, following the edition used. The wording echoes Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit of the Lord rests on the promised ruler.

verse.text: For none of you should suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer, or as a meddler.
verse.note: This word occurs nowhere earlier in surviving Greek and its meaning is uncertain. Its parts suggest “one who oversees what belongs to others”, and most translations render it “meddler” or “busybody”. Other proposals include an embezzler of property held in trust, or someone who interferes in others’ affairs in a way that provokes public hostility.

verse.text: But if anyone suffers as a Christian, let that person not be ashamed, but glorify God in this name.
verse.note: The word occurs only three times in the New Testament (also Acts 11:26 and 26:28) and was probably coined by outsiders as a label for followers of Christ. Here it appears as a charge or taunt for which a person might suffer, and the letter tells readers to bear “this name” without shame. Later manuscripts read “in this matter” instead of “in this name”.

verse.text: For it is time for the judgment to begin with the house of God; and if it starts with us first, what will be the end of those who disobey the good news of God?
verse.note: The Greek word can mean a household or a building, and “house of God” was a common phrase for the temple. The letter has already called its readers a “spiritual house” (2:5), so both senses are probably in play. The idea of judgment beginning at God’s sanctuary echoes Ezekiel 9:6.

verse.text: And “if the righteous person is saved only with difficulty, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?”

note.term: “if the righteous person is saved only with difficulty, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?”
note.traditional: if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?

verse.note: This is Proverbs 11:31 quoted from the Greek Septuagint, which differs from the Hebrew (“If the righteous is repaid on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner”). The adverb means “with difficulty” or “barely”, picking up the thought that even God’s own people pass through judgment.

verse.text: So then, those who suffer according to the will of God should also entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
So I appeal to the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and as one who also shares in the glory that is about to be revealed:
shepherd the flock of God that is among you, watching over it not under compulsion but willingly, as God would have it; not out of greed for gain but eagerly;
verse.note: This participle is missing from some important early manuscripts, and so is the phrase rendered “as God would have it”; editors are divided on whether they are original. The verb is related to the noun for “overseer” (traditionally “bishop”), so the elders here are described as doing an overseer's work.

verse.text: not lording it over those allotted to you, but becoming examples to the flock.

note.traditional: those in your charge; God's heritage (KJV)

verse.note: The Greek word means a lot or an allotted portion, here in the plural. Most interpreters take it to mean the portions of the flock assigned to each elder's care, which “those in your charge” expresses more loosely. The rendering here keeps the idea of allotment, since the people are assigned to the elders and are not theirs to own.

verse.text: And when the chief shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.

note.traditional: crown of glory that fadeth not away

verse.note: The image is the wreath awarded to victors in the games or to citizens publicly honored, which was woven from leaves or flowers and soon withered. This one does not fade. The adjective may also suggest the amaranth, a flower proverbial for not wilting.

verse.text: In the same way, you who are younger, submit to the elders. And all of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, because “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
verse.note: The same Greek word means both “older men” and “elders” as community leaders. Because verses 1–4 address elders as leaders, the word is rendered the same way here, but the contrast with “you who are younger” leads some to read simply “those who are older.”
The verb is rare and means to tie or fasten a garment on oneself. Some connect it with the apron a slave tied on for work, which would suit the context, but that association is not certain.

note.term: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

verse.note: The quotation is Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek version, with “God” in place of “the Lord.” The same line is quoted in James 4:6.

verse.text: Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the proper time,
casting all your anxiety on him, because he cares about you.
Be sober-minded; keep watch. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, looking for someone to devour.
verse.note: The word for “adversary” ordinarily meant an opponent in a lawsuit, though it could be used of an enemy in general. “Devil” renders a Greek word meaning “slanderer” or “accuser,” which the Greek Old Testament used for the figure of Satan, so the courtroom image may be deliberate.

verse.text: Resist him, firm in the faith, knowing that your brothers and sisters throughout the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering.

note.term: your brothers and sisters throughout the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering
note.traditional: the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world

verse.note: The Greek has a collective noun, traditionally “brotherhood,” meaning the whole community of fellow believers, men and women alike. The verb usually means “to accomplish” or “to complete,” and some take the clause to mean that the same sufferings are being brought to completion in, or laid upon, the community. The overall sense, that the readers' sufferings are shared by believers everywhere, is not in doubt.

verse.text: And the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself, after you have suffered a little while, restore you, make you firm, strengthen you, and set you on a foundation.
To him be the power forever and ever. Amen.
verse.note: The Greek has no verb. It can be read as a wish (“to him be”) or as a statement (“to him belongs”); the similar doxology at 4:11 has “is,” which favors the statement, but the traditional wish form is kept here. The noun means might or ruling power.

verse.text: Through Silvanus, the faithful brother, as I regard him, I have written to you briefly, appealing to you and testifying that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it.
verse.note: The phrase can mean that Silvanus carried the letter, or that he helped to write it as a secretary. Comparable expressions in early Christian letters usually refer to the bearer, but both views are held. Silvanus is generally identified with the Silas who traveled with Paul.

verse.text: She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you, and so does Mark, my son.

note.term: She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you
note.traditional: She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen; the church that is at Babylon (KJV)

verse.note: The Greek is a feminine expression with no noun, most often understood as the church in the place from which the letter is sent. “Babylon” is widely taken as a name for Rome, as in Revelation and other Jewish writings of the time, picking up the letter's theme of believers as exiles. A minority understand “she” as an individual woman, or Babylon as a literal place.

verse.text: Greet one another with a kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
